children: "THIS PRICE WAS SET BY AN ALGORITHM USING YOUR PERSONAL DATA."
If you live in New York, you may have seen this disclosure at checkout when shopping online and in stores. If you live elsewhere, it might be coming to your area soon.

Several attorneys general are pursuing surveillance pricing bans or reform bills aimed at protecting consumers from "predatory" personalized pricing similar to New York's, which was implemented in November. The Federal Trade Commission recently followed suit with a policy proposal that could lead to the prosecution of undisclosed personalized pricing-prices set on a buyer-by-buyer basis, often using consumer data-as unfair or deceptive.
These are noble aims, especially as affordability tops Americans' list of concerns. But these measures miss the mark-and it isn't clear that they would fix any demonstrable problem.

Maryland's ban applies only to tax-exempt groceries sold by large grocers and delivery apps, and it carves out temporary discounts, promotional offers, subscription pricing, prices justified by supply and demand, seasonality, perishability, location, shipping costs and, above all, loyalty and rewards programs. New Jersey requires grocery stores to publicly post "uniform pricing benefits" for its loyalty members. At the same time, the state effectively bans targeted coupons-the single form of personalization that most consumers demonstrably like and happily opt in to receive.

If individualized pricing is the problem in need of a fix, food prices are a strange place to start; airlines, hotels, and ride-share platforms move their prices constantly and by far greater dollar amounts. Groceries just have more political salience right now.

What Americans really want is a sense of fairness when shopping, a feeling that they aren't being price gouged for a gallon of milk to compensate for someone else's discounted gallon. The way to achieve fairness, according to the FTC and some states, is uniform pricing: Everyone pays the same price, regardless of their spending capacity or behavior.

In a recent paper, the economists Stefano DellaVigna and Matthew Gentzkow show that U.S. retail chains set nearly identical prices across stores, despite enormous differences in local incomes. Measured against locally optimized prices, they estimate that the poorest neighborhoods pay about 10 percentage points more than the richest. No state legislature has ever held a hearing on national price uniformity, even though it might be moving more money between income groups than personalized pricing could.
In June, Colorado Gov. Jared Polis vetoed a bill on personalized pricing for exactly this reason, warning it would punish "differentially lower prices, not just higher prices."

Evidence supports Polis' claim. In a field experiment at ZipRecruiter conducted by University of Chicago marketing professors Sanjog Misra and I, personalized prices raised profit about 19% over the best possible uniform price. More than 60% of customers paid less than they would have under that uniform price.

The FTC and the states may be addressing a problem that doesn't actually exist. The FTC's 2025 report on surveillance pricing is routinely cited as proof of some hidden epidemic of price gouging. It documents instances of companies buying tools to surveil consumers but not a single instance of a company actually personalizing prices based on surveillance. A decade of academic audit studies of e-commerce finds plenty of "steering"-reordering search results-and coarse segmentation by device or geography, but very little true individual-level pricing.

There is a legitimate discussion to be had around surveillance pricing, but it has to do with consent, not pricing. Firms have bought third-party personal data for marketing since long before the smartphone: credit bureaus, mailing-list brokers, insurance scoring, catalog cooperatives. Americans' rights over their data shouldn't vary on whether the data buyer uses the file to set a price rather than to target an ad, and they shouldn't stop at the supermarket door. Write a disclosure-and-consent rule for the economy. Don't write a grocery statute and call it privacy law.

Perhaps Americans' real grievance isn't that firms use data for personalized pricing but that they are excluded from the behind-the-scenes market to buy their data. In the United Kingdom, Tesco launched its Clubcard in 1995, offering 1% back in exchange for giving the store a record of what items go into their baskets. Shoppers have been "selling" their data for coupons ever since, at a price nobody negotiated. The question is whether they would consent to targeted offers if they could see the terms and share the gains.

That won't be answered by the proposals and laws at hand in the U.S. Maryland's arrives this fall; the most likely consequence is a compliance memo, a disclosure banner and a grocery bill that looks exactly as it did the week before. New Jersey's will be met with lawsuits. Neither will add a discount.
